doc.title: Von Freeman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: First job, society and reflections on time
title: The Depression, rock and roll and changing times
summary: He says hard times erased racial barriers, and that rock and roll displaced jazz as times change.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: And then the Depression evened out a lot of stuff.
Prohibition had been repealed at that time, by that point?

Right. The Depression, like ’26, ’27. ’28, and ’29, that cooled out a lot of people, because a lot of people lost everything they had. It’s just like, say, floods, like when they had all these floods in Texas and things. Everybody just got together, forgot about race, because the floods and things are bigger than anybody. You see mother nature come through and tear up everything, and all the hurricanes and stuff. People just forget about color. It’s more about surviving against these terrific forces. So I think that’s what happened. Now I saw something like what you’re talking about during [?], the ’60s, when rock-and­ roll came in. Rock-and-roll took out jazz. It was so many people playing music that didn’t even know music, but if you could sing or do anything and get a record out there that was good rock, you had it made. This cause a whole lot of problems. A lot of musicians got to disliking one another, which was really silly, because times change, and when times change, time is greater than any man. When times change, hey, if you don’t jump on the bandwagon, then you got to wait for time to change again. It may be – you may be long gone before it change, because who knows when – because I remember when jazz musicians were – people were running around, getting their autographs and stuff. When you’d play, people would invite you over for dinner. They had all your little records, if you didn’t have out but two records. Everybody had a – that was a common thing. Everybody had all Count Basies, all [?]. Everybody had all the big bands’ records. Now, you go over to somebody’s house, they may never play a big band. Times have changed. The rock cats came in. Another thing, they was keeping that beat. Everybody

likes to move. Nobody has forgotten yet how to move. And what a lot of that listening music, with everybody doing like this, like in a trance, that was cool, but a lot of folks was out there shaking booties. That’s what’s happening now. Where this will end, I don’t know.
